question: What is aeromicrobiology mainly about?

options.A: The measurement of atmospheric temperature and pressure
options.B: The study of living microbes floating in the air
options.C: The chemical composition of industrial smog
options.D: The treatment of chronic lung diseases in hospitals

explanation: Spot on! Aeromicrobiology simply looks at microorganisms that travel or hang out in the atmosphere for a bit. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h1)

question: Where do most microbes found in the air come from?

options.A: Chemical reactions between sunlight and vehicle exhaust
options.B: Purely from indoor sterile laboratory equipment
options.C: They multiply and live permanently in the upper atmosphere
options.D: Soil, water, plants, and human or animal activities

explanation: Correct! Microbes aren't actually born in the sky. They get swept up from the ground, water, or living things around us. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why are tiny air particles like PM2.5 so dangerous to our health?

options.A: They react with sunlight to form ozone gas
options.B: They bypass upper airway filters and reach deep lung tissues
options.C: They create a visible yellow haze over industrial cities
options.D: They dissolve completely in the saliva inside the mouth

explanation: Great job! Because they are so tiny, PM2.5 particles slip right past our nose and throat defenses and go straight into the tiny air sacs in our lungs. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h2)

question: If a neighborhood near a busy road and a power plant has high levels of toxic gases, where are those gases mainly coming from?

options.A: Agricultural crop dusting and livestock farming
options.B: Indoor cooking using traditional firewood stoves
options.D: Natural evaporation of stagnant surface water

explanation: Exactly! Power plants pump out industrial emissions, while cars and trucks release vehicle exhaust. Simple as that! [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h2)

question: What exactly is a bioaerosol?

options.A: An airborne particle made up of living organisms or their fragments
options.B: A sterile water droplet found inside hospital oxygen tanks
options.C: An artificial chemical spray used to kill indoor mold
options.D: A gaseous pollutant released exclusively by vehicle exhaust

explanation: Spot on! Think of bioaerosols as tiny living things—like bacteria, fungal spores, viruses, or pollen—just hitching a ride in the air. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h3)

question: How do certain bacteria and fungi manage to survive harsh sun and dry air up in the atmosphere?

options.A: They grow wings to fly away from sunny areas
options.B: They absorb all the pollution particles to feed themselves
options.C: They immediately transform into non-living chemical gases
options.D: They produce protective structures like spores or thick outer coats

explanation: Correct! Spores and tough coats act like a shield, keeping microbes safe until they land somewhere nice. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h3)

question: How do microbes mainly get around from place to place in the air?

options.B: Magnetic pulls from the earth's core

explanation: You got it! Microbes can't fly on their own, so they completely rely on wind and moving air to carry them. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h4)

question: Why can poor ventilation systems be dangerous in a hospital?

options.A: They trap bioaerosols and allow infectious droplets to accumulate
options.B: They make the hospital rooms too cold for patients to recover
options.C: They increase the chemical purity of the air to dangerous levels
options.D: They cause air pressure to drop so low that patients cannot breathe

explanation: Spot on! Without fresh air moving things out, germs stay trapped indoors, increasing the risk of spreading infections to patients and staff. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h4)

question: What happens in our lungs when we breathe in irritating particles?

options.A: White blood cells are recruited, leading to inflammation and mucus production
options.B: Air sacs expand permanently and never deflate again
options.C: Blood flow to the lungs stops completely to protect the heart
options.D: The lung tissue instantly becomes immune to all future infections

explanation: Great! When irritants enter, our immune system steps in, causing swelling and extra mucus, which makes breathing a bit tougher. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h5)

question: An asthmatic patient starts wheezing and coughing after spending the afternoon outside on a heavy smog day. What caused this attack?

options.A: Inflammation and bronchoconstriction caused by inhaled air pollutants
options.B: An allergic reaction to pollen-free chemical gases
options.C: A sudden bacterial invasion of the bloodstream
options.D: Complete destruction of the heart valves due to low oxygen

explanation: Correct! Smog irritates sensitive airways, making the muscles around them tighten up and swell, which triggers asthma symptoms. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h5)

question: Which simple device is used to check how fast a patient can forcefully blow air out of their lungs?
explanation: Spot on! A peak flow meter is a handy little tool nurses use to keep an eye on airflow in asthma patients. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h6)

question: What does an arterial blood gas (ABG) test tell us about a patient exposed to heavy air pollution?

options.A: How well the lungs are managing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange
options.B: The patient's daily exposure level to outdoor traffic exhaust
options.C: The presence of bacterial spores inside the throat
options.D: The exact count of white blood cells in the lungs

explanation: You got it! An ABG test checks how effectively the lungs are taking in oxygen and getting rid of carbon dioxide. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h6)

question: Why does sitting a breathless patient up in a semi-Fowler's or high-Fowler's position help them?

options.A: It stops blood from flowing too quickly to the brain
options.B: It prevents dust particles from settling inside the windpipe
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any supplemental oxygen
options.D: It expands the chest cavity and eases the work of breathing

explanation: Brilliant! Sitting upright uses gravity to pull the diaphragm down, giving the lungs more room to fill up with air. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h7)

question: A hospitalized patient with chronic bronchitis is struggling to breathe and their oxygen is dropping. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.A: Elevate the head of the bed and assess breathing status
options.B: Wait for the environmental agency to clear the outdoor air
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately so they can get fresh air
options.D: Encourage the patient to perform heavy physical exercise

explanation: Spot on! Always start by positioning the patient to help them breathe better and checking their status before jumping to other steps. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a good public health way to reduce air pollution?

options.A: Creating urban green spaces with trees and vegetation
options.B: Encouraging the use of cleaner public transportation options
options.C: Placing strict regulations on factory and industrial emissions
options.D: Increasing the burning of solid wood fuels in open household fires

explanation: Correct! Burning wood in open fires actually makes indoor and outdoor air much worse, so public health programs try to reduce it. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h8)

question: How do parks and tree-lined streets help clean up city air?

options.A: They increase the temperature of the city to destroy bacteria
options.B: They absorb carbon dioxide and trap dust particles
options.C: They produce chemical gases that neutralize industrial smoke
options.D: They block all wind currents so microbes cannot travel

explanation: You nailed it! Plants act like natural filters, taking in carbon dioxide and catching dust right on their leaves. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h8)
